claim: Class B G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) comprise a family of 15 transmembrane receptors that respond to endocrine factors and regulate vital functions in mammals, including glucose and calcium homeostasis, pain transmission and gastrointestinal regulation.
source: G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) of class B comprise a family of 15 transmembrane receptors that respond to endocrine factors and regulate vital functions in mammals, including glucose and calcium homeostasis, pain transmission and gastrointestinal regulation (Bortolato et al., 2014; Wootten et al., 2017; Culhane et al., 2015; Pal et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Bortolato et al., 2014; Wootten et al., 2017; Culhane et al., 2015; Pal et al., 2012).

claim: Class B GPCRs are defined by a large, glycosylated N-terminal extracellular domain (ECD, ~120–160 residues in length) in addition to the heptahelical architecture of the transmembrane domain (TMD) common to all GPCRs.
source: In addition to the heptahelical architecture of the transmembrane domain (TMD) common to all GPCRs, class B receptors are defined by a large, glycosylated N-terminal extracellular domain (ECD, ~120–160 residues in length) (Culhane et al., 2015; Pal et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Culhane et al., 2015; Pal et al., 2012).

claim: The native ligands of class B GPCRs are long peptide hormones, which bear distinct functional sites at the two termini.
source: The native ligands of class B GPCRs are long peptide hormones, which bear distinct functional sites at the two termini (Pal et al., 2012; Beyermann et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Pal et al., 2012; Beyermann et al., 2000).

claim: The C-terminal portion of class B GPCR peptide ligands forms selective high-affinity interactions with the ECD and drives selective receptor binding, while the N-terminal segment interacts with the TMD and triggers receptor activation (two-domain binding model).
source: The C-terminal portion of the peptide forms selective high-affinity interactions with the ECD and drives selective receptor binding, while the N-terminal segment interacts with the TMD and triggers receptor activation (two-domain binding model) (Culhane et al., 2015; Pal et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2014; Beyermann et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Culhane et al., 2015; Pal et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2014; Beyermann et al., 2000).

claim: Crystal structures have revealed the binding mode of ligand C-termini to the isolated ECDs of several class B receptors, but they excluded TMDs.
source: Thus, crystal structures have revealed the binding mode of ligand C-termini to the isolated ECDs of several class B receptors, but they excluded TMDs (Bortolato et al., 2014; Pal et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Bortolato et al., 2014; Pal et al., 2012).

claim: TMD structures for the glucagon receptor and the corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) receptor type 1 (CRF1R) were solved, but they lack the ECDs and represent the receptors in an inactive state bound to allosteric small molecule inhibitors.
source: TMD structures for the glucagon receptor and the corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) receptor type 1 (CRF1R) were also solved, but they lack the ECDs and represent the receptors in an inactive state bound to allosteric small molecule inhibitors (Hollenstein et al., 2013; Jazayeri et al., 2016; Siu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Hollenstein et al., 2013; Jazayeri et al., 2016; Siu et al., 2013).

claim: The full-length crystal structure of the glucagon receptor in complex with a small molecule acting as negative allosteric modulator was solved.
source: Most recently, the full-length crystal structure of the glucagon receptor in complex with a small molecule acting as negative allosteric modulator (Zhang et al., 2017) and the cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the calcitonin receptor in complex with a Gs-protein heterotrimer were also solved (Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Zhang et al., 2017).

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the calcitonin receptor in complex with a Gs-protein heterotrimer was solved.
source: Most recently, the full-length crystal structure of the glucagon receptor in complex with a small molecule acting as negative allosteric modulator (Zhang et al., 2017) and the cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the calcitonin receptor in complex with a Gs-protein heterotrimer were also solved (Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Liang et al., 2017).

claim: High flexibility in the calcitonin receptor cryo-EM complex prevented structure determination of the peptide agonist and ECD part of the complex.
source: While the complex used for cryo-EM included a peptide agonist and the ECD, high flexibility prevented structure determination in this part of the complex, thus highlighting the limitations of structural approaches that require conformational rigidity in the protein, and leaving interaction modes of peptide agonists and antagonists with full-length class B GPCRs unresolved.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the description of the cryo-EM structure limitations.

claim: It is a general feature of class B natural agonists that they turn into partial agonists and then into antagonists by successively truncating residues at the N-terminus.
source: It is a general feature of class B natural agonists that they turn into partial agonists and then into antagonists by successively truncating residues at the N-terminus.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: CRF1R is a key regulator in stress response by triggering the release of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) in the pituitary gland.
source: As prototype class B receptor, we used the CRF1R, which is a key regulator in stress response by triggering the release of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) in the pituitary gland (Bale and Vale, 2004; Stengel and Taché, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Bale and Vale, 2004; Stengel and Taché, 2014).

claim: In humans, CRF1R is activated by the two 41- and 40-mer endogenous peptide agonists CRF and Urocortin I (Ucn1).
source: In humans, CRF1R is activated by the two 41- and 40-mer endogenous peptide agonists CRF and Urocortin I (Ucn1).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: N-terminal truncation of the first eight residues of CRF yields antagonists retaining some weak partial activity, such as CRF(9-41).
source: N-terminal truncation of the first eight residues of CRF yields antagonists retaining some weak partial activity, such as CRF(9-41) (Rivier et al., 1984; Rivier and Rivier, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Rivier et al., 1984; Rivier and Rivier, 2014).

claim: Signaling is completely lost by truncating 11 residues from CRF, as in [DPhe12, Nle21,38]-CRF(12-41) and Astressin.
source: Signaling is completely lost by truncating 11 residues, as in [DPhe12, Nle21,38]-CRF(12-41) and Astressin (Gulyas et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Gulyas et al., 1995).

claim: The binding mode of the agonist Ucn1 on the CRF1R was previously revealed.
source: Although we have recently revealed the binding mode of the agonist Ucn1 on the CRF1R (Coin et al., 2013, 2011), receptor interactions with peptide antagonists remain enigmatic.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous studies (Coin et al., 2013, 2011).

claim: Sub-nanomolar EC50 values for the two agonists CRF and Ucn1 agree with literature data.
source: Sub-nanomolar EC50 values for the two agonists CRF and Ucn1 agree with literature data (Rivier and Rivier, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Rivier and Rivier, 2014) and references experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: dFXCRF(12-41) did not elicit any significant receptor activation up to the maximal tested concentration of 100 nM.
source: As expected, dFXCRF(12-41) did not elicit any significant receptor activation up to the maximal tested concentration of 100 nM, while CRF(9-41) and Ucn1(8-40) showed minimal residual activity (<10%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cAMP accumulation assays shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: CRF(9-41) and Ucn1(8-40) showed minimal residual activity (<10%).
source: As expected, dFXCRF(12-41) did not elicit any significant receptor activation up to the maximal tested concentration of 100 nM, while CRF(9-41) and Ucn1(8-40) showed minimal residual activity (<10%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cAMP accumulation assays shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: All truncated peptides right shifted the dose-response curve of their parent agonist and behaved as competitive antagonists.
source: All truncated peptides right shifted the dose-response curve of their parent agonist and behaved as competitive antagonists (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Azi was incorporated into CRF1R in response to an amber stop codon using a dedicated amino-acyl tRNA synthetase/tRNACUA pair.
source: Azi was incorporated into CRF1R in response to an amber stop codon using a dedicated amino-acyl tRNA synthetase/tRNACUA pair (Coin et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Coin et al., 2013).

claim: 119 positions spanning the whole juxtamembrane region of CRF1R were systematically mapped, with the sole exclusion of eight known non-tolerant sites.
source: We systematically mapped 119 positions spanning the whole juxtamembrane region of CRF1R, with the sole exclusion of eight known non-tolerant sites (Coin et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Coin et al., 2013) and describes the experimental approach.

claim: All Azi-CRF1R mutants showed expression levels in the same order of magnitude, with variations of 0.3–0.9-fold with respect to the wild-type receptor.
source: All mutants showed expression levels in the same order of magnitude, with variations of 0.3–0.9-fold with respect to the wild-type receptor.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two different patterns of crosslinking footprints were observed: one shared by the two agonists and a different one for the three antagonists.
source: Overall, we observed two different patterns of crosslinking footprints: one shared by the two agonists and a different one for the three antagonists (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E, 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The hits obtained with the agonist CRF overlapped with those of the agonist Ucn1.
source: The hits obtained with the agonist CRF overlapped with those of the agonist Ucn1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The crosslinking hits of the 33-mer antagonists CRF(9-41) and Ucn1(8-40) were almost identical to each other.
source: Likewise, the crosslinking hits of the 33-mer antagonists CRF(9-41) and Ucn1(8-40) were almost identical to each other.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The shorter antagonist dFXCRF(12-41) shared the pattern of the 33-mer antagonists with the exception of helix V, where it lacked any hits.
source: The shorter antagonist dFXCRF(12-41) shared the pattern of the 33-mer antagonists with the exception of helix V, where it lacked any hits.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Agonist and antagonist footprints differed for hits in ECL2, helix V and VI, whereas all ligands gave a similar pattern in the hinge region, helix I, II, III, VII and ECL3.
source: Agonist and antagonist footprints differed for hits in ECL2, helix V and VI, whereas all ligands gave a similar pattern in the hinge region, helix I, II, III, VII and ECL3.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 2.

claim: In ECL2, agonists gave a distinct cluster of three hits (K262ECL2, P264ECL2, G265ECL2) versus the four successive hits found for the antagonists (F260ECL2, G261ECL2, K262ECL2, R263ECL2).
source: In ECL2, agonists gave a distinct cluster of three hits (K262ECL2, P264ECL2, G265ECL2) versus the four successive hits found for the antagonists (F260ECL2, G261ECL2, K262ECL2, R263ECL2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In helix V, the 33-mer antagonists featured intense hits (Y2725.39, Q2735.40 and I2775.44) one helix turn deeper than the mapped agonist hits.
source: In helix V, the 33-mer antagonists featured intense hits (Y2725.39, Q2735.40 and I2775.44) one helix turn deeper than the mapped agonist hits.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Hits I3256.51 and T3266.52 in helix VI were visible only for the longer antagonists and are located one helix turn below the prominent hits L3296.55 and F3306.56 found with all ligands.
source: Similarly, hits I3256.51 and T3266.52 in helix VI were visible only for the longer antagonists and are located one helix turn below the prominent hits L3296.55 and F3306.56 found with all ligands.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Three hits at the tip of helix V (D2695.36, Y2705.37 and Y267ECL2) were accessible for the two agonists, but were missing for all three antagonists.
source: Notably, three hits at the tip of helix V (D2695.36, Y2705.37 and Y267ECL2, the latter two pointing out of the TMD in the 3D structure) (Hollenstein et al., 2013) were accessible for the two agonists, but were missing for all three antagonists.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and a citation to the crystal structure (Hollenstein et al., 2013).

claim: Out of the 37 designed Cys-CRF1R mutants, 35 were expressed on the cell surface and retained the ability to bind CRF1R ligands.
source: Out of the 37 designed Cys-CRF1R mutants, 35 were expressed on the cell surface and retained the ability to bind CRF1R ligands, as demonstrated by photo-labeling with the Bpa12-Ucn1 ligand (Kraetke et al., 2005; Coin et al., 2013) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and citations to previous studies (Kraetke et al., 2005; Coin et al., 2013).

claim: All agonists tolerated the introduced Lys(ClAc) substitutions except for [Lys(ClAc)12]-CRF.
source: As demonstrated by cAMP accumulation assays, all agonists tolerated the introduced substitutions except for [Lys(ClAc)12]-CRF, which was excluded from further experiments (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The Lys(ClAc) substitutions were well tolerated by the antagonists, which behaved essentially like dFXCRF(12-41) both in the cAMP accumulation assay and in photo-crosslinking experiments with Azi-CRF1R mutants.
source: The Lys(ClAc) substitutions were well tolerated also by the antagonists, which behaved essentially like dFXCRF(12-41) both in the cAMP accumulation assay and in photo-crosslinking experiments with Azi-CRF1R mutants (Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The C-terminus of the agonist and the antagonist gave identical pair-wise hits with the CRF1R ECD (A31-E104ECD and S33-Y73ECD).
source: The C-terminus of the agonist and the antagonist gave identical pair-wise hits with the CRF1R ECD (A31-E104ECD and S33-Y73ECD).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both CRF and dFXCRF(12-41) featured the pair-wise hit V18-V1201.40.
source: Likewise, both peptides featured the pair-wise hit V18-V1201.40.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: From E17 on toward the N-terminus, the two-dimensional crosslinking fingerprints of agonist and antagonist differ, showing different interaction sets with the receptor.
source: However, from E17 on toward the N-terminus, the two-dimensional crosslinking fingerprints of agonist and antagonist differ, showing different interaction sets with the receptor.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Pair-wise crosslinking experiments revealed 7 proximal pairs of ligand-receptor amino acids for the CRF-CRF1R complex and 15 pairs for the dFXCRF(12-41)-CRF1R complex.
source: Overall, pair-wise crosslinking experiments revealed 7 proximal pairs of ligand-receptor amino acids for the CRF-CRF1R complex and 15 pairs for the dFXCRF(12-41)-CRF1R complex (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Table 2.

claim: The Cβ-Cβ distance for the reaction between Lys(ClAc) and Cys to take place should not exceed 10 Å.
source: Based on the geometry of the Lys(ClAc) moiety, we estimate that the Cβ-Cβ distance for the reaction between Lys(ClAc) and Cys to take place should not exceed 10 Å.
evidence: The claim is based on geometrical estimation shown in Figure 4A and Monte Carlo sampling experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For hits obtained with [ClAc0]-dFXCRF(12-41), the maximal distance is estimated at 5 Å between the Nα of the peptide and the Cβ of the receptor residue.
source: For hits obtained with [ClAc0]-dFXCRF(12-41), which bears the ClAc moiety on the N-terminus, we estimate a maximal distance of 5 Å between the Nα of the peptide and the Cβ of the receptor residue (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on geometrical estimation shown in Figure 4A and Monte Carlo sampling experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Docked CRF forms a long α-helical segment from the C-terminus to residue V18.
source: Docked CRF forms a long α-helical segment from the C-terminus to residue V18 (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular model shown in Figure 5.

claim: The C-terminal segment (I41-V18) of CRF binds to the CRF1R ECD similarly to the crystal structure of CRF1R ECD bound to CRF(26-41) (PDB: 3EHU).
source: The C-terminal segment (I41-V18) binds to the CRF1R ECD similarly to the crystal structure of CRF1R ECD bound to CRF(26-41) (PDB: 3EHU) (Pioszak et al., 2008), and approaches the TMD antiparallel to the helical stalk of helix I.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the molecular model with a crystal structure (PDB: 3EHU) cited from Pioszak et al., 2008.

claim: Experimental constraints L15-Q1732.68, H13-F3306.56 and H13-F3447.38 impose disruption of the α-helical conformation and the formation of a short loop in the segment R16-L14 of CRF.
source: As CRF enters the TMD in the groove formed by the helices I, II and VII, experimental constraints L15-Q1732.68, H13-F3306.56 and H13-F3447.38 impose disruption of the α-helical conformation and the formation of a short loop in the segment R16-L14.
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular model constrained by experimental pair-wise crosslinking data.

claim: Following the loop at R16-L14, docked CRF shows a second α-helical segment (H13-S7) that lies across the TMD interface.
source: Following this loop, docked CRF shows a second α-helical segment (H13-S7) that lies across the TMD interface.
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular model shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ligand CRF reaches six of the seven TM helices as deep as Y1241.44, W1692.64, H1993.40, Q2735.40, L3296.55 and S3497.43.
source: The ligand reaches six of the seven TM helices as deep as Y1241.44, W1692.64, H1993.40, Q2735.40, L3296.55 and S3497.43 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular model and experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No interactions are predicted by the CRF-CRF1R model with helix IV, in accord with the absence of any experimental crosslinking in this helix.
source: No interactions are predicted by the model with helix IV, in accord with the absence of any experimental crosslinking in this helix.
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular model and the absence of experimental crosslinking data for helix IV.

claim: The very N-terminus of CRF (I6-S1) exits the binding pocket through a gap between helix V and VI and extends beyond the TMD.
source: Finally, the very N-terminus of CRF (I6-S1) exits the binding pocket through a gap between helix V and VI and extends beyond the TMD.
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular model shown in Figure 5.

claim: The conformation of the docked CRF agonist is similar to the conformation adopted by Ucn1 in the Ucn1-CRF1R model from a previous study.
source: Overall, the conformation of the docked CRF agonist is similar to the conformation adopted by Ucn1 in the Ucn1-CRF1R model in our previous study (Coin et al., 2013), even though the two models are based on distinct and independent sets of experimental constraints.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the current model with a previous model (Coin et al., 2013) shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Ucn1 model predicted the kink in the α-helical fold of the agonist at the entrance of the TMD pocket even without pair-wise crosslinks in this region.
source: Notably, the Ucn1 model predicted the kink in the α-helical fold of the agonist at the entrance of the TMD pocket even without pair-wise crosslinks in this region, while new experimental constraints further enforce this conformation in CRF (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with a previous model (Coin et al., 2013) and the current model shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both agonist models predict a modest 3.1 Å inward shift of the extracellular tip of helix VII and a movement of ECL3, which compacts the orthosteric binding pocket around the peptide with respect to the crystal structure of the CRF1R TMD bound to CP-376395.
source: Both agonist models predict a modest 3.1 Å inward shift of the extracellular tip of helix VII and a movement of ECL3, which compacts the orthosteric binding pocket around the peptide with respect to the wide-open conformation observed in the crystal structure of the CRF1R TMD bound to the small molecule antagonist CP-376395 (PDB: 4K5Y) (Hollenstein et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the molecular models with the crystal structure (PDB: 4K5Y) cited from Hollenstein et al., 2013.

claim: This compaction of the binding pocket results from receptor flexibility at the 'backbone hinges' Q3557.49 and G3567.50 and at ECL3.
source: This compaction results from receptor flexibility at the 'backbone hinges' Q3557.49 and G3567.50 and at ECL3, leads to an overall gain in the conformational energy of the complex and helps to satisfy the pair-wise distance restraints.
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular modeling approach and analysis of the model.

claim: The TMD model of the CRF-CRF1R complex satisfies the Ucn1 restraints in the Ucn1-CRF1R model and vice versa, so that the two models strongly validate each other.
source: Importantly, the TMD model of the CRF-CRF1R complex, based only on restraints identified in this study, satisfies the Ucn1 restraints in the Ucn1-CRF1R model and vice versa, so that the two models strongly validate each other (Table 3).
evidence: The claim is based on cross-validation of the models shown in Table 3.

claim: The only substantial difference between CRF and Ucn1-bound CRF1R models is found in the ECD domain, which is now rotated and shifted about 5 Å.
source: The only substantial difference between CRF and Ucn1-bound CRF1R models is found in the ECD domain, which is now rotated and shifted about 5 Å.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the models shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Docked dFXCRF(12-41) antagonist shows both similarities and major differences compared to the conformation of CRF agonist.
source: Docked dFXCRF(12-41) antagonist shows both similarities and major differences compared to the conformation of CRF agonist (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the molecular models shown in Figure 5.

claim: The C-terminal segments (I41-V18) of both agonist and antagonist similarly interact with CRF1R ECD, the hinge region and the helical stalk of helix I.
source: The C-terminal segments (I41-V18) of both agonist and antagonist similarly interact with CRF1R ECD, the hinge region and the helical stalk of helix I, which accounts for identical patterns of pair-wise restraints and Azi-footprints in these regions (Figures 1–3, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular models and experimental data shown in Figures 1–3 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: While the C-terminal segment of CRF agonist kept the α-helical conformation up to E17 inclusively, the α-helix in the dFXCRF(12-41) antagonist already unravelled at residue E17.
source: As a consequence, while the C-terminal segment of CRF agonist kept the α-helical conformation up to E17 inclusively, the α-helix in the dFXCRF(12-41) antagonist already unravelled at residue E17.
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular models shown in Figure 5.

claim: From E17, docked dFXCRF(12-41) keeps the non-helical conformation all the way up to its N-terminal residue (dF12).
source: From E17, docked dFXCRF(12-41) keeps the non-helical conformation all the way up to its N-terminal residue (dF12), which accounts for the series of antagonist-specific pair-wise crosslinking in this region, including crosslinking of L15 with R3417.35 and I3457.39, crosslinking of L14 with N1231.43 and crosslinking of H13 with L3296.55, F3306.56 and F3447.38.
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular model and experimental pair-wise crosslinking data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: While the N-terminal segment of the CRF agonist is solvent exposed outside the pocket, the N-terminus (dF12) of the dFXCRF(12-41) antagonist is buried inside the TMD.
source: Finally, while the N-terminal segment of the CRF agonist is solvent exposed outside the pocket, the N-terminus (dF12) of the dFXCRF(12-41) antagonist is buried inside the TMD, which is corroborated by chemical crosslinking of dF12 with L3296.55, F3306.56 and N3487.42 (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular models and experimental pair-wise crosslinking data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The predicted conformation of the TMD orthosteric pocket in the dFXCRF(12-41)-CRF1R model is much more compact compared to both the CRF1R crystal structure and the agonist-bound complexes.
source: Compared to both the CRF1R crystal structure and the agonist-bound complexes, the predicted conformation of the TMD orthosteric pocket in the dFXCRF(12-41)-CRF1R model is much more compact (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the molecular models shown in Figure 6.

claim: Backbone flexibility at the 'backbone hinges' Q3557.49 and G3567.50 led to a dramatic inward shift of the extracellular tips of helices VI and VII by ~6 Å and ~9 Å, respectively, in the dFXCRF(12-41)-CRF1R model compared to the small-molecule bound TMD crystal.
source: Backbone flexibility at the 'backbone hinges' Q3557.49 and G3567.50 and extensive conformational sampling of the TMD helical bundle in the modeling procedure led to a dramatic inward shift of the extracellular tips of helices VI and VII by ~6 Å and ~9 Å, respectively, as compared to the conformation of the small-molecule bound TMD crystal (PDB: 4K5Y) (Hollenstein et al., 2013) (Figure 6A, red arrows indicate the inward shift) .
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular model and comparison with the crystal structure (PDB: 4K5Y) cited from Hollenstein et al., 2013, shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The shift of helices VI and VII in the antagonist-bound model was accompanied by a shift in the ECL3, which formed a 'lid' on top of the N-terminal segment of the bound antagonist.
source: This shift of the helices was also accompanied by a shift in the ECL3, which formed a 'lid' on top of the N-terminal segment of the bound antagonist.
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular model shown in Figure 6.

claim: Conformational changes of the TMD predicted in the flexible dFXCRF(12-41)-CRF1R model are critical for explaining the Azi photo-crosslinking results.
source: Therefore, conformational changes of the TMD predicted in the flexible dFXCRF(12-41)-CRF1R model are critical for explaining the Azi photo-crosslinking results, which were employed to validate the model.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the modeling results and validation with experimental data.

claim: The models predict two distinct conformations for the TMD of CRF1R when bound to either agonist or antagonist, defined as 'wide' and 'compact', respectively.
source: Overall, our models predict two distinct conformations for the TMD of CRF1R when bound to either agonist or antagonist, which we define as 'wide' and 'compact', respectively (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular models shown in Figure 6.

claim: The CRF1R complex with CRF agonist maintained integrity in all restrained and unrestrained MD runs, with all seven amino acid pairs involved in chemical crosslinking retaining a close proximity throughout the simulation.
source: The CRF1R complex with CRF agonist maintained integrity in all restrained and unrestrained runs, with all seven amino acid pairs involved in chemical crosslinking retaining a close proximity throughout the simulation (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In unrestrained MD runs of the CRF-CRF1R complex, some residue pairs dynamically fluctuated in and out of the range of 10 Å, which is compatible with the crosslinking reaction.
source: In unrestrained runs, some residue pairs (e.g. H13-F3447.38) dynamically fluctuated in and out of the range of 10 Å, which is compatible with the crosslinking reaction.
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The CRF1R complex with dFXCRF(12-41) antagonist maintained overall integrity in both restrained and unrestrained simulations, with most of the 15 distances determined with pair-wise crosslinking being retained within 10–12 Å.
source: The CRF1R complex with dFXCRF(12-41) antagonist also maintained overall integrity in both restrained and unrestrained simulations (Figure 7B,C), with most of the 15 distances determined with pair-wise crosslinking being retained within 10–12 Å.
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: MD simulations showed higher flexibility for the linear N-terminal segment of the antagonist in respect to the homologous α-helical segment of the agonist.
source: Thus, simulations showed higher flexibility for the linear N-terminal segment of the antagonist in respect to the homologous α-helical segment of the agonist.
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7.

claim: MD showed that the 'wide' TMD conformation is less optimal than the 'compact' conformation for CRF1R interactions with the dFXCRF(12-41) antagonist.
source: Therefore, MD showed that the 'wide' TMD conformation is less optimal than the 'compact' conformation for CRF1R interactions with the dFXCRF(12-41) antagonist (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both the agonist- and the antagonist-bound models showed overall flexibility throughout the MD simulations.
source: Interestingly, while preserving inter-residue contacts, both the agonist- and the antagonist-bound models showed overall flexibility throughout the simulations.
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The orientation of the ECD relative to the TMD was especially variable, swaying as much as 15–20 Å relative to the membrane normal during MD simulations.
source: Especially variable was the orientation of the ECD relative to the TMD, which swayed as much as 15–20 Å relative to the membrane normal (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 9A,B.

claim: High flexibility in MD simulations was observed for ECL3.
source: High flexibility in MD simulations was also observed for ECL3.
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Residue E336ECL3, located about 14 Å away from the ligand in the CRF-CRF1R model, came as close as ~6 Å to the peptide during 800 ns simulation runs, thus explaining occurrence of Azi photo-crosslinking at this position.
source: Residue E336ECL3, located about 14 Å away from the ligand in the CRF-CRF1R model, came as close as ~6 Å to the peptide during 800 ns simulation runs, thus explaining occurrence of Azi photo-crosslinking at this position (Figure 1, Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 9C and experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: High flexibility of ECL3 is supported by the crystal structure of the CRF1R TMD, where only one of the three molecules composing the crystallographic unit shows well defined electron density for ECL3.
source: High flexibility of ECL3 is also supported by the crystal structure of the CRF1R TMD, where only one of the three molecules composing the crystallographic unit shows well defined electron density for ECL3 (Hollenstein et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the crystal structure (Hollenstein et al., 2013).

claim: Crosslinking results provide direct evidence that N-truncated antagonists of CRF1R extensively penetrate the TMD.
source: Our crosslinking results provide direct evidence that N-truncated antagonists of CRF1R extensively penetrate the TMD, which explains previous observations obtained with chimeric constructs and isolated receptor domains (Hoare et al., 2004, 2005), as well as the fact that the 30-mer antagonist Astressin induces CRF1R internalization (Perry et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental crosslinking data shown in Figures 1-3 and citations to previous studies (Hoare et al., 2004, 2005; Perry et al., 2005).

claim: CRF1R antagonists give a different footprint on the receptor TMD compared to the natural agonists CRF and Ucn1, revealing distinct interactions with helix V, helix VI and with ECL2.
source: Compared to the natural agonists CRF and Ucn1, however, CRF1R antagonists give a different footprint on the receptor TMD, revealing distinct interactions with helix V, helix VI and with ECL2.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental crosslinking data shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: While agonists protrude into a groove between helices V and VI, the 33-mer peptides do reach both helices but do not penetrate through them.
source: While agonists protrude into a groove between helices V and VI, the 33-mer peptides, which behave as weak partial agonists at high concentration, do reach both helices (Azi-hits Y2725.39, Q2735.40, I2775.44, I3256.51) but do not penetrate through them (lack of crosslinking at Y267ECL2, D2695.36, Y2705.37).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental crosslinking data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The 30-mer antagonist dFXCRF(12-41), which is not able to activate the receptor at all, shows no contact with helix V, although it maintains contacts with other helices.
source: The 30-mer antagonist dFXCRF(12-41), which is not able to activate the receptor at all, shows no contact with helix V, although it maintains contacts with other helices.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental crosslinking data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Distinct agonist and antagonist footprints suggest a role for ECL2 in CRF1R activation.
source: Distinct agonist and antagonist footprints suggest also a role for ECL2 in CRF1R activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental crosslinking data shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: ECL2 is known for contributing to ligand binding in CRF1R.
source: Indeed, ECL2 is known for contributing to ligand binding in CRF1R (Assil-Kishawi and Abou-Samra, 2002; Gkountelias et al., 2009), and a number of studies suggested a role of ECL2 in activation of class B GPCRs (Koole et al., 2012) and other GPCRs (reviewed in [Wheatley et al., 2012]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Assil-Kishawi and Abou-Samra, 2002; Gkountelias et al., 2009; Koole et al., 2012; Wheatley et al., 2012).

claim: Comparison of the atomistic models of CRF1R bound either to CRF or dFXCRF(12-41) shows a different folding for the agonist and the antagonist in the CRF1R TMD, as well as different conformations of the receptor.
source: Comparison of the atomistic models of CRF1R bound either to CRF or dFXCRF(12-41) shows a different folding for the agonist and the antagonist in the CRF1R TMD, as well as different conformations of the receptor.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the molecular models shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: While CRF resumes the helical folding from H13 on, the N-terminus of dFXCRF(12-41) keeps an extended conformation.
source: However, while CRF resumes the helical folding from H13 on, the N-terminus of dFXCRF(12-41) keeps an extended conformation.
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular models shown in Figure 5.

claim: The linear N-terminus of the antagonist shows higher flexibility in MD simulations as compared to the corresponding α-helical region of agonist, which suggests weaker and less defined interactions with the receptor.
source: The linear N-terminus of the antagonist shows higher flexibility in MD simulations as compared to the corresponding α-helical region of agonist, which suggests weaker and less defined interactions with the receptor and explains the ~10 fold lower binding affinity of CRF1R to dFXCRF(12-41) than to CRF (Gulyas et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7 and a citation to a published study (Gulyas et al., 1995).

claim: CRF1R TMD compacts around the unstructured N-terminal segment of the antagonist, while it adopts a more open conformation to accommodate the bulkier α-helical segment and the N-terminal tip of the agonist.
source: Thus, CRF1R TMD compacts around the unstructured N-terminal segment of the antagonist, while it adopts a more open conformation to accommodate the bulkier α-helical segment (S7-H13) and the N-terminal tip (S1-I6) of the agonist, which protrudes between helices V and VI beyond the pocket (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular models shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Stabilization of a wide open TMD conformation is important for the activation of CRF1R by peptide agonists.
source: Apparently, stabilization of such a wide open TMD conformation is important for the activation of CRF1R by peptide agonists.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the molecular models and experimental data.

claim: The crystal structure of CRF1R TMD bound to the allosteric antagonist CP-376395 features an even more open V-shape than the agonist-bound models.
source: Interestingly, the crystal structure of CRF1R TMD bound to the allosteric antagonist CP-376395 (PDB: 4K5Y) (Hollenstein et al., 2013) features an even more open V-shape.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with the crystal structure (PDB: 4K5Y) cited from Hollenstein et al., 2013.

claim: CP-376395 sits deep in the TMD closer to the G-protein-binding site and likely blocks the signal transmission via a mechanism that is distinct from the action of orthosteric peptide antagonists.
source: However, CP-376395 sits deep in the TMD closer to the G-protein-binding site and likely blocks the signal transmission via a mechanism that is distinct from the action of orthosteric peptide antagonists (Hollenstein et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and a citation to a published study (Hollenstein et al., 2014).

claim: Movements of the extracellular parts of helices VI and VII rely on Glycine hinges G3246.50 and G3567.50, which are fully conserved among class B GPCRs.
source: Movements of the extracellular parts of helices VI and VII rely on Glycine hinges G3246.50 and G3567.50, which are fully conserved among class B GPCRs.
evidence: The claim is based on the molecular models and knowledge of sequence conservation.

claim: Hinge flexibility in the apo state and stabilization of a specific conformation of helices VI and VII upon agonist binding can be relevant for the activation mechanism of other class B receptors.
source: Therefore, hinge flexibility in the apo state and stabilization of a specific conformation of these helices upon agonist binding (Figure 6) can be relevant also for the activation mechanism of other class B receptors.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the molecular models and knowledge of sequence conservation.

claim: The extracellular motions of helices VI and VII in the models for binding of a class B agonist are likely converted into intracellular motions of these helices.
source: The extracellular motions of helices VI and VII in our models for binding of a class B agonist are likely converted into intracellular motions of these helices, corroborating the notion that a global displacement of helices VI and VII is a key feature of GPCR activation in general.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the molecular models and general knowledge of GPCR activation.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the calcitonin receptor in complex with the Gs-protein heterotrimer provides the first structural evidence for the conformational changes occurring in the intracellular part of a class B helical bundle.
source: While our crosslinking approach reveals details of conformational changes in the ligand-binding pocket of a class B GPCR, the recently solved cryo-EM structure of the calcitonin receptor in complex with the Gs-protein heterotrimer (PDB: 5UZ7) (Liang et al., 2017) provides the first structural evidence for the conformational changes occurring in the intracellular part of a class B helical bundle.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the cryo-EM structure (PDB: 5UZ7) from Liang et al., 2017.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the calcitonin receptor confirms that class B GPCR activation involves a large-scale movement of helix VI, which shapes the site for G-protein binding and activation.
source: Specifically, it confirms that class B GPCR activation, similar to class A (Katritch et al., 2014), involves a large-scale movement of helix VI, which shapes the site for G-protein binding and activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the cryo-EM structure (Liang et al., 2017) and a study on class A GPCRs (Katritch et al., 2014).

claim: According to the active-like CRF-CRF1R model, helical rearrangement involves a sharp kink around the conserved G6.50 flexible hinge in helix VI, resulting in the outward movement of both extracellular and intracellular tips of helix VI.
source: Note, that according to our active-like CRF-CRF1R model, this helical rearrangement involves a sharp kink around the conserved G6.50 flexible hinge in helix VI, resulting in the outward movement of both extracellular and intracellular tips of helix VI.
evidence: The claim is based on the active-like molecular model shown in Figure 8.

claim: The stability of the active-like conformation of the CRF-CRF1R complex observed in MD simulations suggests that such dramatic rearrangements can be relevant for the activation mechanism of CRF1R, and potentially of other class B GPCRs.
source: The stability of this active-like conformation of the CRF-CRF1R complex observed in MD simulations suggests that such dramatic rearrangements can be relevant for the activation mechanism of CRF1R, and potentially of other class B GPCRs.
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 8 and inference about the activation mechanism.

claim: CRF1R peptide antagonists extensively interact with the receptor TMD, but stabilize a different conformational state in respect to the agonists.
source: We show that CRF1R peptide antagonists extensively interact with the receptor TMD, but stabilize a different conformational state in respect to the agonists.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental crosslinking data and molecular models shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: All experimental data are obtained from the intact full-length, fully glycosylated receptor at the membrane of the live cell.
source: Notably, all our experimental data are obtained from the intact full-length, fully glycosylated receptor at the membrane of the live cell, and do not require a rigid conformation of the complex to determine the ligand-receptor interactions.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental approach described in the Materials and methods section.
